area: Area IV. Preflight Lesson on a Maneuver to be Performed in Flight
objective: By the end of this lesson you can build and deliver a preflight lesson on any maneuver the evaluator picks from Areas VI to IX: work from a lesson plan that has every essential item, state a measurable objective, describe the maneuver's elements and common errors for full and partial panel, choose instructional aids that fit instrument training, and explain how you recognize, analyze and correct each error. You also get one complete sample lesson and a checklist to build your own library of maneuver lessons.
why: When Area IV is part of the test, the CFII PTS has the evaluator pick at least one maneuver from Areas VI through IX and ask you to present a preflight lesson on it the way you would teach it to a student; lesson plans from your own library may be used (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area IV NOTE). Instrument maneuvers are taught to a learner who cannot see out and has little spare attention, so the explaining has to happen on the ground: the AIH puts the explanation phase before the flight lesson, with the objectives, completion standards and a thorough preflight briefing [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. The IFH lesson guide calls it vitally important to brief the student on each lesson's objective and how it will be accomplished [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

warmup: Think first: the evaluator says, "I am your instrument student. I have flown partial panel straight-and-level and turns. Teach me recovery from unusual attitudes before we go fly." You have your plan, a marker board and a model airplane. What do you say in the first two minutes, what is the one thing the student must be able to do at the end, and which mistake do you most want to stop before it happens?

key_terms.def: An organized outline for a single instructional period: it tells the instructor what to do, in what order, and what procedure to use [[25:212|AIH G-4]].
A measurable statement of the learner's desired performance, made of a description of the skill or behavior, the conditions and the criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].
An objective that develops judgment and ADM through dynamic, meaningful scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]; the focus shifts to these as the learner progresses [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

The criteria of the lesson objectives; listing the criteria sets the completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Plans may call them assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

The first phase of demonstration-performance, done before the flight lesson: objectives, completion standards, a thorough preflight briefing, the precise actions, the end result, safety procedures and questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Instructor tells and demonstrates; learner tells while the instructor does; learner explains while doing; instructor evaluates while the learner performs [[25:215|AIH G-7]].
Devices that assist the instructor; they are not self-supporting but support, supplement or reinforce what is taught [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
What is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, which is why an instructor needs to teach it correctly the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
Flying with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; on an electronic flight display, with the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].
An airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight; except in training it is not intentional, so it is often unexpected [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
Learner self-assessment followed by the instructor's detailed assessment and a discussion comparing the two; also called learner-centered grading [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Area IV: what the evaluator asks for, and when

body.p: Area IV has one Task. The NOTE in the CFII PTS (FAA-S-8081-9E) says the evaluator selects at least one maneuver from Areas VI through IX and asks you to present a preflight lesson on it **as the lesson would be taught to a student**. Previously developed lesson plans from your own library may be used. The PTS calls the Task an exhibit of instructional knowledge of the selected maneuver, shown five ways:

head: PTS item
What the evaluator listens for
Where this lesson teaches it
rows: K1 Using a lesson plan that includes all essential items
An organized plan that you clearly know, fitted to the student
K3 Accurate, comprehensive oral description, with elements and common errors
The maneuver in the order flown, full panel and partial panel, each element with its error
K4 Using instructional aids, as appropriate
Aids chosen for the key points, not decoration
K5 Describing the recognition, analysis and correction of common errors
For each error: what it looks like, why it happens, the fix

body.p: **Instructional knowledge** has a set meaning in the PTS introduction: your discussions, explanations and descriptions should follow the teaching procedures and techniques of the Aviation Instructor's Handbook, including scenario-based lessons, evaluating SRM and learner-centered grading. The current edition is FAA-H-8083-9B; the AIH describes a lesson plan as a guide that tells the instructor what to do, in what order and by what procedure [[25:212|AIH G-4]].

**When it is tested.** On an initial test the PTS has the evaluator select one or more Tasks in each Area of Operation, so Area IV is tested under its NOTE. The PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor certificate marks Area IV "N" (not required) for every certificate and rating held, and the renewal or reinstatement table requires 1 Task from Area IV. Either way, these plans are the same ones you use every day: lesson plans are designed to assure that each learner receives the best possible instruction [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

callout.text: The CFI version of this Task is lesson AI.IV.A, with slow flight and rectangular course examples. The FOI lessons FOI.I.G (Planning Instructional Activity) and FOI.I.C (Teaching Process) teach lesson plans and the teaching process in depth. This lesson applies them to instrument maneuvers and the five items of the CFII PTS.

check.q: You hold a CFI with an airplane rating and are adding the instrument rating. Must the evaluator give you an Area IV preflight lesson?
check.a: No. The PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating marks Area IV not required. It is required on a renewal or reinstatement test (1 Task), and the plans are your everyday teaching tools anyway, since they assure each learner the best possible instruction [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

chunks.title: K1: a lesson plan with all the essential items

body.p: **Using a lesson plan that includes all essential items to make an effective and organized presentation** (K1). Writing a plan means, in effect, that you have taught the lesson to yourself before teaching it to a learner [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Whatever the format, every aviation lesson plan includes objectives, content to support them, and completion standards; the headings vary, and completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Plans for one-on-one training may be quite simple [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

The AIH says the parts of a good objective fill in much of the plan: the elements of the lesson, the schedule, the equipment, the instructor and learner actions, and the completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. For an instrument maneuver, those items look like this:

head: Essential item
What it holds for an instrument maneuver
Source
rows: What the learner will do, under what conditions (full or partial panel, view-limiting device) and how well
The steps in the order they are flown, each with its instrument picture and its common error
Ground brief, the flight segments, the postflight
Airplane and POH/AFM, view-limiting device, a way to cover or fail the gyro instruments, figures, a training device
You explain, demonstrate, supervise and evaluate; the learner tells, then tells and does
The objective's criteria, set for this learner's stage
Safety procedures, exchange of flight controls, risk discussion

body.p: Figure 7-6 is the AIH's traditional plan: an objective, completion standards, and content split into preflight discussion, review, introduction and postflight discussion [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. Its completion standard says "within a specified limit" of heading, altitude and airspeed [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. In your own plan, write the actual limits for the learner you describe.

Then check the plan against the characteristics of a well-planned lesson: unity, content (new material tied to the previous lesson, with a short review), scope (a person can master only a few principles or skills at a time), practicality (planned for the airplane or ground trainer and the aids actually available), and flexibility [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]; relation to the course of training, and the four instructional steps [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

callout.text: Every plan: objective, content, completion standards. Then test it: unity, content, scope, practicality, flexibility, relation to the course, instructional steps.

check.q: Your plan for partial-panel unusual attitudes also covers steep turns, compass turns and holding. Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson does it break?
check.a: Scope. A person can master only a few principles or skills at a time, and too much material confuses [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

chunks.title: Using the plan, and where the maneuver fits

body.p: **How to use a lesson plan properly:** be familiar with it, use it as a guide, adapt it to the learner and revise it periodically [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. A plan keeps you from getting off track, omitting essential points and introducing irrelevant material [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. A flight lesson plan should fit the background, flight experience and ability of the particular learner, and may have to be changed considerably or even abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

Commercially developed plans are acceptable for flight instructor applicants on practical tests, but even well-designed preprinted plans may need to be modified [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Whichever you use, the AIH expects you to study each step and be thoroughly familiar with the subject [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

**Where the maneuver fits.** The IFH Instrument Training Lesson Guide is meant for developing lesson plans; its lessons follow a building-block sequence, and each includes ground training for its flight portion [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Partial panel operations are Lesson 6, recovery from unusual attitudes with partial panel practice is Lesson 7, and intercepting, tracking and holding are Lesson 8 [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. Students should master each lesson's objective before moving on [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

**Organize it** as introduction (attention, motivation, overview), development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]] [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Develop the main points past to present, simple to complex, known to unknown, or most used to least used [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. After writing the plan, rehearse it, ideally with another instructor watching as critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

callout.text: Application: put a learner profile at the top of each plan (instrument hours, last lesson, airplane and panel). If the evaluator describes a different student, say out loud what you will change. The explanation phase is based on the learner's known experience and knowledge [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

check.q: Your library plan for holding was written for a learner with 25 hours of instrument time. The evaluator says to brief a learner who has just finished partial panel work. What does the AIH say about your plan?
check.a: Adapt it. A flight lesson plan should fit the particular learner's background, experience and ability, and may need considerable change [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The IFH guide also puts holding after the partial panel and unusual attitude lessons [[23:343|IFH B-2]].

body.p: **Stating the objective** (K2). Say it early: the overview in the introduction is a clear, concise presentation of the objective and the key ideas, a road map of the lesson [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. Knowing what is expected can ease a significant source of uncertainty and frustration for the learner [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

A **performance-based objective** has three parts: a description of the skill or behavior, the conditions, and the criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Avoid phrases such as "knowledge of" and "awareness of," which cannot be measured [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Conditions give the equipment, references and limits; if someone asks "But what if ...?", they need clarifying. Criteria leave no question whether the performance meets the objective [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

head: Part
Weak
Stronger (instrument example)
rows: "Recognize a nose-high or nose-low unusual attitude and recover to straight-and-level flight" [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Under a view-limiting device, full panel, then with the attitude and heading indicators covered" [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]
"Names the attitude before any control input, applies the IFH recovery sequence, then returns to the assigned altitude" [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]

body.p: **Decision-based objectives** develop judgment and ADM through realistic scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], and the AIH says to shift toward them as the learner's performance rises [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. An instrument example (application): given a vacuum failure in simulated IMC, the learner spots the failure, uses the instruments that still work and advises ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

**Set the criteria for this learner.** ACS and PTS standards cover only the most critical tasks and are not a whole syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]; lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed them before checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Learner-centered grading gives you words for a level: Describe, Explain, Practice, Perform, or Not observed [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

callout.text: Application: say the objective in one sentence, write it on the board and leave it there. Come back to it at the end, because the conclusion relates the important elements to the objective [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

check.q: An applicant opens with: "Today you will gain an awareness of partial panel flying." What is wrong with it?
check.a: "Awareness of" cannot be measured, and there are no conditions or criteria. A performance-based objective names a measurable behavior, its conditions and its criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

chunks.title: K3: an accurate, comprehensive oral description

body.p: **Giving an accurate, comprehensive oral description of the maneuver, including the elements and associated common errors** (K3). In AIH terms, this is the explanation phase: convey the precise actions the learner will perform, describe the end result, cover the safety procedures, and invite questions on any step [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
What "comprehensive" means for an instrument maneuver:

bullets: **Full panel and partial panel.** The PTS introduction says Area VI is taught with the full panel and with partial panel or backup instruments. Except for the instrument takeoff, every analog maneuver in the IFH can be flown with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and every maneuver on an electronic display with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].

**One method, named.** The Area VI NOTE has you select primary and supporting or control and performance. Both use the same instruments and control responses and differ in how much they rely on the attitude indicator [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
**This airplane.** IFH techniques must be modified to suit each aircraft, using its POH/AFM [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

**The order flown.** Explain a skill in the same step-by-step order used to perform it; go known to unknown when it builds on earlier maneuvers, simple to complex when several skills are taught together [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
**Plain words.** Avoid jargon and technical terms the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
**Numbers.** In the demonstration you will explain the power settings and attitudes [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], so put them in the description first.

body.p: For each element, give the learner three things: the instrument picture, the control input, and the result to expect. That is instrument interpretation as the IFH defines it: knowing how each instrument works and applying it to the airplane, the maneuver and the conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

**Where the errors come from.** Many PTS Tasks list their own common errors; the PTS says they may or may not be found in the references and are there because they happen often. The IFH adds lists after most maneuvers, for example straight-and-level flight [[23:173|IFH 7-12]], turns [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] and unusual attitudes [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Put them in the preflight description: what is learned first leaves an almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], faulty habits are hard to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]], and a learner who is briefed on errors and told how to correct them can make progress [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

callout.text: Application: accurate means current and checked. Take every number from the current IFH and the POH/AFM of the airplane you will fly [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], not from memory of another airplane.

check.q: You brief steep turns on the full panel only. The student will fly a trainer with an electronic flight display. What did your description leave out?
check.a: Partial panel. On an electronic display every maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]], and the PTS steep turn Task asks for the full panel and partial panel procedure.

chunks.title: K4: instructional aids for instrument maneuvers

body.p: **Using instructional aids, as appropriate** (K4). Aids are not self-supporting: they support, supplement or reinforce what you teach, and relatively simple aids that cover the key points are best [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. "As appropriate" has a practical test in the AIH: use an aid on a key point, where a technical description would be long, where a point is hard to put into words, where you find yourself forming visual images, or where the learner is puzzled [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. Keep the words on an aid to a minimum and do not use aids as a crutch [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

rows: Draw the panel and the order of reading; erase and redraw for each element; the learner can draw too
Panel figures give you and the learner the same visual image, such as IFH Figures 7-39 and 7-40
The learner sees how to fly it and the performance criteria from the start
Shows attitude and bank; easy to handle and good for questions
Ground instruction need not be in a classroom; sit in the airplane and point to each instrument and its power source
Most instrument rating tasks can be taught first in an FFS, FTD or ATD
Covering failed instruments may help a pilot keep control; the IFH flies partial panel with the gyro instruments covered

body.p: **Limits.** The FAA recommends training in the simulator until the tasks are done successfully, before trying them in the aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], but ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests [[25:173|AIH 9-3]]. For upset recovery, the AFH says only Level C and D full flight simulators are a satisfactory substitute for skill development in the airplane [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. If a two-dimensional picture does the job, use it rather than a model [[25:130|AIH 5-27]], and check every aid for technical accuracy before you use it [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].

check.q: Why might a printed IFH panel figure work better than a spoken description of a nose-low attitude?
check.a: Aids belong where a point is hard to put into words or where you find yourself forming visual images [[25:127|AIH 5-24]], and pictures give instructor and learner a common visual image [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

body.p: **Describing the recognition, analysis, and correction of common errors** (K5). The PTS includes common errors so the evaluator can see whether you can recognize, analyze and correct them. In flight the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers and simulates errors, but will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). In Area IV you describe that process on the ground; the flight Tasks of Areas VI to IX test it in the air.

head: Step
What you do
Source
rows: Know what the error looks like on the instruments. Watch the learner's eyes: a long look at one instrument may be fixation; a gaze that never reaches the engine instruments may be inattention. Looking is not the same as seeing

Find the cause. With the learner thinking aloud you can tell an error caused by a misconception from a simple lack of motor skill. A fixation may come from trouble with interpretation or control, not only the scan
Identify the error, explain it and tell how to fix it; give concrete suggestions. If it needs reteaching: demonstrate, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate

body.p: **Let the learner find the way out.** Safety permitting, it is often better to let learners go part of the way into a mistake and find a way out; a learner who seldom corrects an error has trouble learning the maneuver [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. When a learner flies it right but may not understand why, have the learner vary it, combine it with other operations or apply it to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

**Errors chain together under the hood.** The IFH example: a pilot fixates on an altimeter 200 feet low, tension builds on the controls, and an unnoticed heading change follows [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Application: brief the first error in the chain, because in the IFH example one error leads to the next.

callout.text: Application: describe each error in three short lines the student can remember: "You will see ... It happens because ... Fix it by ..."

check.q: Your learner rolls the wrong way twice during partial-panel recoveries. Before you correct it, what do you want to know, and how do you find out?
check.a: Whether it is a misconception or a motor-skill problem. Have the learner say each step aloud while flying; thinking aloud shows which it is [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Risk: the safety items every instrument brief carries

body.p: The explanation phase includes appropriate safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], and risk management belongs in all preflight and postflight briefings, with learners leading more of it as they gain experience [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. An unprepared learner is a serious hazard; a thorough briefing before each training flight is part of the mitigation [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. These items go in every instrument maneuver plan:

bullets: **Exchange of flight controls.** The preflight briefing should include the exchange procedure, and the positive three-step exchange is strongly recommended [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]: "You have the flight controls," "I have the flight controls," "You have the flight controls," with a visual check [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The PTS lists it as a special emphasis area.

**Safety pilot.** Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat with at least a private certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

**View-limiting device.** On a practical test the applicant furnishes a device that blocks the applicant's outside view [[60:225|14 CFR 61.45(d)(2)]]; the PTS asks applicant and evaluator to agree and brief when and how it goes on and comes off.

**Weather margin.** The weather must be good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and the pilot's concentration on the instruments, with more margin near a busy airway or airport [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].
**See and avoid.** Vigilance is required under IFR or VFR whenever the weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]; practice see and avoid at all times in training [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

**Altitude and area.** For stall practice the IFH asks for a safe altitude above the terrain, no conflicting traffic, suitable weather and radar traffic advisories [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; disorientation demonstrations are never flown at low altitude or without an instructor or safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].
**Distractions.** Tell the learner you will add realistic distractions; the AIH lists examples such as resetting the clock or finding a heading on a chart [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

callout.text: Guard the controls and be ready to take them. Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and learners should never be allowed to exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Visibility is legal but hazy near a busy airport, and today the learner will spend most of the flight under the hood. What does the AIM say?
check.a: Be sure the weather is good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and the pilot's concentration on the instruments, and give yourself more margin near a busy airway or airport [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].

chunks.title: Sample lesson, parts 1 and 2: the plan and the objective

body.p: **This lesson's own example**, built from the sources; it is not an FAA lesson plan. Maneuver: recovery from unusual flight attitudes, full panel and partial panel (Area VI Task H, which the Area VI NOTE says the evaluator shall select). The pilot's side is in IR.IV.B and the instructor depth in FII.VI.H; this sample shows how to package it for Area IV.

**Learner, as the evaluator might describe:** an instrument student in a fixed-pitch trainer with a six-instrument panel and a single vacuum pump, who has finished the partial panel lesson, Lesson 6 in the IFH guide [[23:343|IFH B-2]].

Sample entry
rows: Recovery from unusual attitudes with partial panel practice, the content of IFH Lesson 7 [[23:343|IFH B-2]]
A short review of the Lesson 6 partial panel instruments for pitch and bank [[25:152|AIH 7-8]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Ground brief; in flight: clearing, full panel demonstration, learner practice, partial panel demonstration, learner practice; postflight debrief [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]

Airplane and POH/AFM (its recovery procedure, if it has one), view-limiting device, instrument covers, marker board, model airplane, IFH Figures 7-39, 7-40 and 11-8 [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]

Three-step exchange of controls, safety pilot and weather margin, clearing, enough altitude [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
From the objective below; postflight self-assessment, then yours [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

body.p: **Part 2: the objective (K2), said in the overview and written on the board.** Performance-based: "Under a view-limiting device, first with the full panel and then with the attitude and heading indicators covered, you will recognize a nose-high or nose-low unusual attitude that I set up, name it before you move the controls, recover to straight-and-level flight in the IFH order, and return to the assigned altitude" [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

Decision-based, for a later lesson: in a scenario where the attitude indicator quietly fails in simulated IMC, the learner notices the disagreement with the other instruments, covers the failed instruments, keeps control and advises ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

Completion standard for today: the Practice level, where the learner plans and executes and coaching corrects the errors [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. End goal: the instrument rating ACS standard for this Task (FAA-S-ACS-8C, IR.IV.B), reached before checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

callout.text: Objective = behavior + conditions + criteria. Say it first, write it down, come back to it at the end.

check.q: Why does the sample objective require the learner to name the attitude before moving the controls?
check.a: The recovery depends on the type: decreasing airspeed calls for the nose-high recovery, increasing airspeed the nose-low one [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The AFH lists incorrect assessment of the type of upset first among recovery errors [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

chunks.title: Sample lesson, part 3: the oral description

body.p: **Part 3 (K3): the description, element by element, in the order flown.** This is still this lesson's own sample, built from the IFH, not an FAA lesson plan. Application: this is what you say, with the common error you brief at each step.

head: Element
What you tell the learner
Error to brief with it
rows: Turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, preoccupation with flight deck duties, careless cross-checking, interpretation errors and weak aircraft control [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Not keeping the airplane trimmed, and a disorganized flight deck [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]

Any rate or indication that does not belong to a basic maneuver: assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check. The question is what the airplane is doing now, not how it got there [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Slow cross-check and fixation: the impulse to stop and stare at the discrepancy [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]

Power as needed for the deceleration, forward elevator to lower the nose and prevent a stall, then coordinated aileron and rudder to level the miniature aircraft and center the ball. Almost at once, but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. If the stall warning or buffet is already there, fly the stall recovery instead: reduce the angle of attack first, then roll wings level, then add power as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Recovering by body sensations instead of sight [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]

Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, keeping the ball centered, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure. A proficient recovery changes all controls together; in early training, fly it by the numbers in that order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
The instinctive pull on the elevator [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]

Level pitch shows when the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize; straight, coordinated flight shows as a level miniature aircraft and a centered ball on the turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Overcontrol: needles stopping and reversing means passing through level, so keep the cross-check fast [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]

As the airspeed, altimeter and turn coordinator stabilize, bring the attitude indicator back into the cross-check; once stabilized, return to the altitude assigned by the instructor or ATC [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Weak basic skills: every basic instrument error grows during a recovery [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]

body.p: **Full panel note.** In moderate attitudes the attitude indicator gives a quick level reference. A spillable type may have passed its limits, and even a working nonspillable type can be off up to 5 degrees in pitch and bank and is hard to read in extreme attitudes. Start the POH/AFM procedure if there is one; otherwise recover by the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Application: taught that way, the full panel and partial panel recoveries use the same steps.
**The end result to describe:** straight-and-level, coordinated flight, then the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Then ask for questions on any step [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

callout.text: Airspeed falling: power up, nose down, wings level. Airspeed rising: power back, wings level, nose up.

check.q: During your description the student asks why the wings come level before the pull in the nose-low recovery. What do you answer?
check.a: The IFH order for nose-low is power, bank, then smooth back pressure, and it warns that the instinctive reaction is to pull [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. In a banked descent, trying to climb or stop the descent tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Sample lesson, parts 4 and 5: aids and error correction

body.p: **Part 4 (K4): each aid and the key point it supports,** in this lesson's own sample.

head: Aid
Key point it supports
Source
rows: What nose-high and nose-low look like on every instrument
Marker board sketch of the panel
The order of reading: airspeed for pitch direction, turn coordinator and ball for bank
A banked, nose-low airplane, and why the wings come level before the pull
A vacuum failure: missing the off flags can turn a benign failure into a hazardous one
Partial panel practice without the attitude and heading indicators

body.p: Close Part 4 with visualization: the learner talks through a recovery while you add an unexpected change, and you ask questions to check the thinking [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. The AFH notes that upset training can start with classroom visualization of the recovery procedures [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

**Part 5 (K5): recognition, analysis and correction.** The PTS names two errors for this Task, incorrect interpretation of the flight instruments and inappropriate application of controls; the IFH list adds the rest.

head: Error
Recognize: what you see
Analyze: why
Correct: what you do
rows: Controls moved the wrong way for the attitude, such as pushing while airspeed is already rising
Airspeed not read first; a stare at one instrument [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Learner says "airspeed, altimeter, turn" and names the attitude before moving [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
A pull before the wings are level in a nose-low turn; big, abrupt inputs
The instinctive pull [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]; the untrained reaction is abrupt muscular effort [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Fly it by the numbers, in order, and watch for overcontrol [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
The airplane wanders as soon as the learner reaches for something
Pressures held instead of trimmed off [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Trim before every task; practice with distractions [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
Head down, hunting for a chart
Hunting for charts, logs or computers pulls attention off the instruments [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Arrange the items for the flight neatly for easy access [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Stops and stares at the odd indication
Not yet trained enough for immediate recognition [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
More recognition drills with the panel figures until the reading is immediate [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Corrects toward what it feels like
A disorientation demonstration, then trust the panel [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]

check.q: The evaluator, playing your student, recovers from a nose-low left turn by pulling hard first. Name the error, its cause and your fix.
check.a: Inappropriate application of controls, from the instinctive pull on the elevator. Fix: power back, level the wings by the turn coordinator, then smooth back pressure, flown by the numbers [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Delivering it: the evaluator as your student

body.p: Present it "as the lesson would be taught to a student" (Area IV NOTE), so teach the evaluator as the learner described. The AIH describes the same role play in instructor training: an instructor plays the learner, and the applicant briefs the maneuver before the flight, demonstrates it and talks the learner through it [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

head: Step
What you do
Source
rows: A question or short story about the maneuver; an unrelated joke distracts
Why it matters to this learner: an unexpected attitude brings an instinctive, not deliberate, reaction unless trained
The objective and the key ideas: the road map
The elements in the order flown, each with its error
Safety procedures, then questions on any step
The learner talks you through it with the model; correct a misunderstanding before the learner is busy flying
Retrace the important elements and relate them to the objective; no new ideas

body.p: The flight then follows Figure 9-7: instructor tells and does, learner tells and instructor does, learner tells and does, learner does and instructor evaluates [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Demonstrate in the same sequence you explained, and if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. After the flight the learner replays, reconstructs, reflects and redirects before you compare assessments [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

callout.text: Application: time each plan when you rehearse it [[25:114|AIH 5-11]], and know which parts you can shorten. No source sets a time limit for the Area IV presentation.

check.q: Why have the learner tell you the recovery steps while you fly the first one?
check.a: Freed from flying, the learner can organize the steps, and you can check understanding and correct a misunderstanding before the learner becomes absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Your library: a plan for every Task in Areas VI to IX

body.p: The evaluator may pick any maneuver in Areas VI to IX, so build one plan per Task, all in the same format, before the test. The PTS's own applicant checklist lists "PTS Lesson Plan" under personal equipment. Use this checklist for each plan:

bullets: 1. **Header:** Task, learner profile, and where it sits in the IFH lesson guide [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]].
2. **Objective:** behavior, conditions (full panel, partial panel or backup instruments) and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].
3. **Completion standards:** today's level of performance and the ACS as the end goal [[25:137|AIH 6-6]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

4. **Elements:** every PTS element of the Task in the order flown, each with its instrument picture and control input; partial panel wherever the Task asks for it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].
5. **Common errors:** the PTS list plus the IFH list, each with recognize, analyze and correct [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
6. **Aids:** one per key point, simple and checked for accuracy [[25:127|AIH 5-24]] [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].
7. **Safety:** exchange of controls, safety pilot, weather margin, see and avoid [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].
8. **Airplane numbers** from the POH/AFM [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].
9. **Postflight:** critique, preview of the next lesson and a study assignment [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].
10. **Revise** when aids, regulations or manuals change [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

head: Task

rows: Pitch, bank and power relationship; full and partial panel; coordination and trim
True airspeed and bank for a standard rate turn; half-standard rate; full and partial panel
Straight and turning flight, full and partial panel; trim
VI.D Constant airspeed climbs and descents

VI.E Constant rate climbs and descents

VI.F Timed turns to compass headings
Compass errors; calibrating the turn coordinator with the clock; full and partial panel
Entry and recovery, full and partial panel; cross-check; roll-in and roll-out; horizon bar precession
Conditions that lead to them; nose-high and nose-low, full and partial panel
VII.A Intercepting and tracking, DME arcs
Tuning and identifying; course setting; position; intercepts; arcs; station passage; failures; MFD use
Equipment, speed, fix, timing, wind, DME, ATC reports; MFD use
Chart, ATC, configuration, MDA and visibility, descent, continue or circle or miss; MFD; one NPA without the gyros (Area NOTE)
The same structure, with DA or DH and equipment status
When to go missed; power, climb attitude, drag; report; procedure; climb gradient
Choosing the maneuver; minimums; visibility; MDA until a normal descent to land
VIII.E Landing from a straight-in approach
Transition to visual flight; advisories; checklist; positive control
Recognizing it; continue or deviate; when to begin the approach
IX.B Loss of primary flight instruments
Recognizing it; telling ATC; a nonprecision approach without the primary instruments

callout.text: Application: the Area NOTEs make some Tasks required anyway (VI.H, VII.A and B, VIII.A and B), so those plans do double duty: they are your Area IV library and your preparation for flying and explaining those Tasks in the air.

check.q: Which Tasks in Areas VI to VIII do the PTS Area NOTEs make the evaluator select?
check.a: Task H and at least one other in Area VI; Tasks A and B in Area VII; Tasks A and B in Area VIII, combined with C, D or E (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area NOTEs). In Area IX at least one Task. Build those plans first, using the IFH lesson guide sequence [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

body.p: These are errors applicants make when they deliver the lesson itself. Each fix comes from the sources.

Reading it word for word, losing the thread

The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]

callout.text: A commercial plan you have not studied shows quickly. The AIH accepts commercial plans for flight instructor applicants, but expects them adapted and expects you to know every step [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

check.q: An applicant's brief on holding ends by introducing DME holds for the first time. What is wrong?
check.a: New ideas do not belong in the conclusion, which should retrace the important elements and relate them to the objective [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

scenario.title: A library plan meets a different airplane
scenario.setup: You are a CFII at a busy school. Your instrument learner, Dana, has about 20 hours of instrument training, all in the school's glass-panel trainers. Today her airplane is down, and the only one free is an older fixed-pitch trainer with a six-instrument panel and a single vacuum pump. The plan is a partial panel nonprecision approach at the towered airport 15 miles away. Visibility is 5 miles in haze, and the approach course crosses a busy airway. Your library plan for this lesson was written for the glass-panel trainer.

questions.q: What do you change in your plan before the brief, and why?
questions.a: Fit it to this learner and this airplane. A flight lesson plan should match the learner's background, experience and ability and may need considerable change [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], and techniques must be modified for each aircraft using its POH/AFM [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. In this airplane, partial panel means the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and Dana has not seen that picture, so add a review of the analog failure picture (IFH Figure 11-8).

questions.q: State a performance-based objective for today.
questions.a: For example: "Under a view-limiting device, with the attitude and heading indicators covered, fly the assigned nonprecision approach to the MDA and a missed approach, holding the course and altitudes in the plan." It has a measurable behavior, the conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Set today's level for her stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

questions.q: Which safety items go in today's brief?
questions.a: The weather must make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with extra margin near the busy airway and airport [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]; you, as safety pilot, need vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]] and see and avoid applies under IFR too [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]; and the three-step exchange of controls is briefed before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: Which aids do you choose, and why those?
questions.a: Aids on the key points only [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]: IFH Figure 11-8 for the vacuum failure picture [[23:333|IFH 11-8]], the approach chart, and a marker board sketch of the six-pack with the gyros crossed out. If a training device is available, practice the procedure there first; the FAA recommends finishing tasks in the simulator before the aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: Dana asks how she would even know the vacuum pump had failed in cloud. What do you teach?
questions.a: A warning indicator, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the supporting instruments, usually shows a failure. Keep control, speed up the cross-check, compare the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and VSI, use the instruments that still work, cover the failed ones, and advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the vacuum gauge belongs in the scan [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

questions.q: After the flight Dana rates her approach "Perform." You had to coach her twice on the stepdown altitudes. How do you handle the debrief?
questions.a: Use collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then yours, then a discussion comparing them [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Needing coaching to correct errors is the Practice level, not Perform [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]; the AIH's own example ends with the learner seeing where more practice is needed [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

skills.do: Deliver a preflight lesson on a maneuver from your library to someone playing your student: state the objective, describe each element in the order flown with its instrument picture, control input and common error, full panel and partial panel, and end by relating the elements to the objective.
skills.practice: Rehearse each plan with another instructor as critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]], with that instructor playing a learner and copying real learner reactions, as in the AIH role play example [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

skills.do: For each common error of the selected maneuver, say aloud how you recognize it on the instruments, what usually causes it, and how you correct it and check the fix.
skills.practice: Take turns flying errors for another applicant in a training device or under the hood with a safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]; the person instructing names the error, asks the learner to think aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] and gives the fix.

quiz.q: Per the Area IV NOTE, what may you bring to present your preflight lesson to the evaluator?
options: Only a blank form that the evaluator supplies on the day
Lesson plans you developed earlier for your library
Nothing; the lesson must be given from memory alone
Only the FAA's own published lesson plan for that Task
quiz.why: The Area IV NOTE in FAA-S-8081-9E says previously developed lesson plans from the applicant's library may be used. The AIH adds that commercially developed plans are acceptable for flight instructor applicants on practical tests, though they may need to be modified [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. None of the sources here gives a ready-made plan for each Task; the IFH guide lists topics by lesson [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

quiz.q: Whatever its format, which three things does the AIH say every aviation lesson plan includes?
options: Objectives, a story for attention, and a written quiz
Content, a risk assessment and the ACS tolerances
An attention step, the content and a study assignment
Objectives, content to support them, and completion standards
quiz.why: All aviation lesson plans should include objectives, content to support the objectives, and completion standards; the headings and names vary [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. A story or question can serve the attention element, but it is not a required part of every plan [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: An applicant's objective reads: "The learner will gain an awareness of partial panel flying." What is the main problem?
options: It is not measurable and has no conditions or criteria
It is too long for a learner to remember during a flight
It should name the evaluator as the person being taught
Objectives belong only in ground lessons, not flight
quiz.why: Phrases like "awareness of" cannot be measured well; a performance-based objective has a description of the behavior, the conditions and the criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Flight lessons need objectives too [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

quiz.q: Your learner will fly a trainer with an electronic flight display. What does partial panel mean for its maneuvers in the IFH?
options: The MFD is turned off while the PFD stays normal
The autopilot flies the airplane in roll mode only
The AHRS is simulated or made inoperative
The standby instruments are covered by the instructor
quiz.why: On an electronic flight display, every maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown partial panel with the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. On analog panels it means the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. Covering the standby instruments would take away the backups, not the primary displays.

quiz.q: Where do the AIH guidelines say instructional aids belong in a lesson?
options: On key points, such as ideas hard to put into words
At the start only, to get the learner's attention
On every single point, so the learner never needs to listen
Only in classrooms, never in one-on-one briefs
quiz.why: Concentrate aids on the key points: long technical descriptions, points that are complex and hard to put into words, when you find yourself forming visual images, or when learners are puzzled [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. Aids support the verbal presentation and are not a crutch [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

quiz.q: Before you leave the explanation phase of a maneuver lesson, what does the AIH say to do?
options: Have the learner fly it once without any help
Grade the learner's skill against the ACS limits
Leave the safety items for the demonstration phase
Invite questions on any step not understood
quiz.why: Before leaving the explanation phase, encourage learners to ask questions about any step they do not understand; the phase also covers the appropriate safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Performance and evaluation come later [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

quiz.q: Your student sees the panel in this figure. Which recovery does the IFH give?
options: Add power, push the nose forward, then level the wings
Reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose
Raise the nose first, then reduce the power
Level the wings, add power, then push forward
quiz.why: Airspeed increasing, altitude decreasing and a diving left turn mean a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The IFH order: reduce power, correct the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Adding power and pushing is the nose-high recovery [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

quiz.q: With the attitude indicator covered, what tells your learner that the airplane has reached level pitch during a recovery?
options: The VSI needle passes through zero for a moment
The turn coordinator's miniature aircraft is level
The airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize
The magnetic compass stops moving and settles
quiz.why: A level pitch attitude is shown by the reversal and stabilization of the airspeed and altimeter needles [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The turn coordinator shows straight, coordinated flight, not pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: The evaluator, as your student, recovers from a nose-low left turn by pulling hard on the yoke first. Which PTS error is it, and what is the fix?
options: Interpretation error: read the attitude gyro first
Trim error: roll in nose-up trim before recovering
Flight deck error: stow the charts, then recover
Control error: power back, wings level, then pull
quiz.why: Pulling first is inappropriate application of controls (PTS VI.H). The instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude is to pull back; the IFH order is power, bank, then smooth back pressure, flown by the numbers in early training [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies the recovery correctly, but you suspect she does not understand why it works. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Have her vary it or combine it with other maneuvers
Sign it off, since correct flying shows understanding
Repeat the identical recovery ten more times
Take the controls each time she starts a recovery
quiz.why: When learners may perform correctly without understanding the principles, have them vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations or apply the same elements to other maneuvers; those who do not understand will probably not manage it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: You plan a lesson on unusual attitude recoveries with partial panel practice. Where does the IFH lesson guide place it?
options: Lesson 2, with preflight preparation
Lesson 8, together with holding practice
Lesson 7, after partial panel work
Lesson 20, with the cross-country flights
quiz.why: Lesson 6 is partial panel operations and Lesson 7 is recovery from unusual attitudes, with partial panel practice in its flight training; holding is in Lesson 8 [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. The guide uses a building-block sequence [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

quiz.q: For a hood lesson, what is the minimum certificate the safety pilot in the other control seat must hold under 14 CFR 91.109(c)?
options: Commercial pilot, with an instrument airplane rating
Private, with category and class ratings for the aircraft
Flight instructor, with an instrument instructor rating
Student pilot, with a current solo endorsement
quiz.why: The safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft (with a narrow sport-instructor exception for solo cross-country training) [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and needs adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: You hold a CFI and are adding the instrument rating. What does the PTS table say about Area IV for you?
options: It is not required for any rating held
It needs two maneuvers instead of only one
It applies only to a CFI-Helicopter
It is replaced by an oral on Area I
final_quiz.why: The PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor certificate marks Area IV "N" for every rating held; the renewal and reinstatement table requires 1 Task (FAA-S-8081-9E). The plans still matter: lesson plans assure each learner receives the best possible instruction [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner arrives having missed the partial panel lesson, but today's plan is partial-panel unusual attitudes. What does the AIH say about the plan?
options: Teach it as written to stay on schedule
Cancel the flight and assign reading only
Modify it, or drop it in favor of review
Teach both lessons at once to catch up
final_quiz.why: A plan may need considerable change because of gaps in the learner's knowledge, and in some cases the entire plan is abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Teaching both at once breaks the scope rule [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Which part of a performance-based objective says "under a view-limiting device, with the attitude and heading indicators covered"?
options: The description of the behavior
The conditions
The criteria
The completion standards
final_quiz.why: Conditions explain the rules for demonstrating the skill: equipment, references and limiting parameters [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. The criteria are the standards that measure accomplishment, and they become the completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the ACS or PTS in your lesson plans matches the AIH?
options: It is the syllabus; teach each Task in listed order
Its tolerances are the standard from lesson one
It removes the need for an objective in each plan
It is a testing tool; lesson standards build up to it
final_quiz.why: The ACS/PTS is not a teaching tool but a testing tool, and lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed it before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Certification tests do not represent an entire syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: After a lesson your learner plans and flies the recoveries, and your coaching corrects her errors. Which learner-centered grade fits?
options: Describe
Explain
Practice
Perform
final_quiz.why: Practice: the learner plans and executes, and coaching, instruction or assistance corrects deviations. Perform means no instructor assistance and errors corrected by the learner [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the telling-and-doing technique, which step lets you catch a misunderstanding before the learner is busy flying?
options: Learner tells, instructor does
Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Learner tells, learner does
final_quiz.why: With the learner telling while you fly, a misunderstanding can be corrected before the learner becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Figure 9-7 marks it as the important transition [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: You catch yourself giving a long spoken description of how the turn coordinator and ball look in a nose-low left turn. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Keep talking; aids suit only classroom groups of learners
Skip it; the learner will see it in the air anyway
Hand over the POH and move to the next step
Use an aid; the point is hard to put into words
final_quiz.why: Aids fit where long technical descriptions are needed or a point is hard to put into words [[25:127|AIH 5-24]], and pictures give instructor and learner common visual imagery [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: Per the AFH, which training devices are a satisfactory substitute for developing upset recovery skills in the airplane?
options: Any basic aviation training device
Level C and D full flight simulators only
Any flight training device of level 4 or higher
Any device that has a working attitude display
final_quiz.why: Only the higher fidelity devices, Level C and D FFS, are a satisfactory substitute; otherwise initial skill development should be in a suitable airplane, with the device building on those skills [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Safety permitting, how does the AIH say to handle a learner's mistake in flight?
options: Let her go partway into it and find the way out
Take the controls as soon as any error appears
Stay silent and save all of it for the debrief
List every error at once, then demonstrate again
final_quiz.why: Correcting errors does not mean taking over the moment a mistake is made; safety permitting, it is often better to let learners progress part of the way into the mistake and find a way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Errors still have to be identified and explained [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: Visibility is legal VFR but hazy, and the practice area is next to a busy airway. What does the AIM say about simulated instrument flight?
options: Legal VFR minimums are all a hood lesson needs
Hood work is not allowed within 5 miles of a busy airway
Only a safety pilot with an instrument rating may be used
Have enough weather margin for the safety pilot's view
final_quiz.why: Be sure the weather is good enough to compensate for the safety pilot's restricted visibility and the pilot's concentration on the instruments, with a little more margin near a busy airway or an airport [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]. The safety pilot needs a private certificate, not an instrument rating [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's eyes stay on the altimeter for a long time while the heading drifts. What is it, and what limit does the AIH put on the eye-watching technique?
options: Omission; the eyes show exactly what she understands now
Emphasis; a long look means the scan is working
Fixation; but looking at it is not the same as seeing
Inattention; it can only be found in the debrief
final_quiz.why: A long look at one instrument may be fixation, and following the eyes helps, but looking in the same direction is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. The IFH gives the same picture: a fixation on the altimeter with tension on the controls and an unnoticed heading change [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner sees an instrument rate that does not belong to any basic maneuver. What does the IFH rule say?
options: Wait for a second instrument to agree before acting
Assume an unusual attitude; cross-check faster
Engage the autopilot and let it fly the recovery
Look outside for the horizon to confirm the attitude
final_quiz.why: Any time an instrument rate of movement or indication other than those of the basic maneuvers is noted, assume an unusual attitude and increase the speed of cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or a malfunction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

final_quiz.q: In IFH Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 feet, not turning left. What does the IFH warn about this picture?
options: Missed flags can make a benign failure hazardous
Vacuum gyros fail all at once, so this is easy to spot
Most small airplanes have a vacuum failure warning light
The turn coordinator always fails along with the gyros
final_quiz.why: Gyros that slow down may wander; a pilot who fails to see the off or failed flags may misread the turn and turn a normally benign situation into a hazardous one [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the gauge belongs in the scan [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

final_quiz.q: What does the Area VI NOTE in the PTS say about the attitude instrument flying method you teach?
options: The evaluator assigns one method at the start of the test
Only control and performance is accepted on glass panels
Both methods must be used together in every Task
You pick primary and supporting, or control and performance
final_quiz.why: The Area VI NOTE lets the applicant select either method for teaching that Area (FAA-S-8081-9E). Both use the same instruments and control responses and differ in their reliance on the attitude indicator [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: What should you avoid in the conclusion of your preflight lesson?
options: Retracing the key elements
Introducing new ideas
Relating them to the objective
Reinforcing what was learned
final_quiz.why: An effective conclusion retraces the important elements and relates them to the objective, which reinforces learning; new ideas should not be introduced because they are likely to confuse the learner [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is giving you the controls back. What does the AIH say she should do?
options: Let go the moment your hands first touch the yoke
Let go as soon as you nod and point to the panel
Keep flying until you say "I have the flight controls"
Let go as soon as she has said the words once
final_quiz.why: When returning the controls, the learner follows the same procedure and stays on the controls, flying the aircraft, until the instructor says "I have the flight controls." There should never be any doubt about who is flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

takeaways: Area IV: at least one maneuver from Areas VI to IX, taught as to a student, from your own plan if you like (not required when adding the instrument rating to a flight instructor certificate).
Every plan has an objective, content and completion standards; test it against the characteristics of a well-planned lesson.
State a measurable objective early: behavior, conditions (full or partial panel) and criteria.
Describe the maneuver in the order flown: the instrument picture, the control input and the common error at each step.
Aids go on key points, stay simple and are checked for accuracy.
For each error: recognize it, find its cause, give the fix.
Every brief carries the exchange of controls, the safety pilot, the weather margin and see and avoid.
Build one plan per Task in Areas VI to IX, in one format, and rehearse each with a critic.
cfi_notes: When Area IV is tested: on an initial test the evaluator selects one or more Tasks in each Area of Operation, so the Area IV NOTE applies; the PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor certificate marks Area IV "N" (not required) for every certificate and rating held; and the renewal and reinstatement table requires 1 Task from Area IV (FAA-S-8081-9E). Tell an applicant which path applies before deciding how much test time the plans need; they are worth building either way, because lesson plans assure each learner the best possible instruction [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

The CFI ACS version of this Task (lesson AI.IV.A) is organized differently: purpose, elements and common errors, desired outcomes and completion standards, risk management, and delivery with a lesson plan, teaching methods and teaching aids. The CFII PTS lists five items, including stating the objective and describing the recognition, analysis and correction of common errors. Before reusing a plan built for AI.IV.A, check that it states the objective and covers how each error is recognized, analyzed and corrected.

The AIH counts the phases of demonstration-performance differently: five in Chapter 5, with learner performance and instructor supervision separate [[25:124|AIH 5-21]], and four in Chapter 9, combining them [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Both say the two happen at the same time [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. FOI.I.C covers this; use the evaluator's wording.

The PTS lists only two errors for unusual attitudes (interpretation and control application), the IFH lists five faults [[23:189|IFH 7-28]] [[23:190|IFH 7-29]], and the AFH lists five upset recovery errors [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. The PTS says its listed errors may or may not be in the references. Brief the PTS two by name and show where the IFH and AFH items fit under them.

Unusual attitude or upset: the AFH says an instructor-set attitude of 30 degrees of bank and 15 degrees nose up is an unusual attitude but not an upset, and with eyes closed the surprise disappears [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Do not let the sample lesson promise upset readiness it does not train.

The PTS references name FAA-H-8083-9 and FAA-H-8083-15 without edition letters and FAA-S-ACS-8 without a revision. Teach and cite the current AIH (FAA-H-8083-9B), IFH (FAA-H-8083-15B) and Instrument ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8C).

In flight the evaluator acts as a student and simulates errors, but not conditions that could jeopardize safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Your Area IV description of recognition, analysis and correction is the script you will use when those errors appear, so keep the two consistent.

Evaluators may ask why the sample recovery starts with airspeed. The IFH answer: the recovery is initiated by reference to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator unless the POH/AFM gives a procedure, because the attitude indicator may have exceeded its limits or failed [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
gaps: No source here sets a time limit, length or required format for the Area IV presentation; the PTS only says previously developed lesson plans may be used.
No source says which maneuvers evaluators pick most often for Area IV, so every Task in Areas VI to IX needs a plan.
The unusual attitude recovery procedure, power settings and the power source of each instrument must come from the airplane's POH/AFM [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
None of the sources here gives a ready-made lesson plan for each CFII Task; the IFH Appendix B guide lists topics by lesson, not full plans [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

No source here says which instrument covers to use or how to simulate an AHRS failure on a particular avionics system; the IFH says only that covering failed instruments may help [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] and that the AHRS is "simulated or rendered inoperative" [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. Agree on the method from the AFM or its supplement before flight.

activities.title: Characteristics of a well-planned lesson
activities.intro: Tap a characteristic, then tap what it looks like in an instrument lesson plan.

pairs.r: Every procedure and aid aims at today's few objectives
New material, tied to last lesson with a short review
Unusual attitudes today; holding waits for another lesson
Planned for the airplane, trainer and aids you really have
Blank space in the outline for add-on material
The learner sees how it serves the instrument rating

activities.why: The characteristics of a well-planned lesson [[25:152|AIH 7-8]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The holding example follows the IFH guide, which puts holding in Lesson 8, after unusual attitudes in Lesson 7 [[23:343|IFH B-2]].

activities.title: Behavior, conditions or criteria?
activities.intro: Tap each piece of an objective, then tap the part of a performance-based objective it belongs to.

items.t: Recover to straight-and-level flight from a nose-low attitude
Navigate from point A to point B
Using appropriate charts, a prepared flight log and a training aircraft
Under a view-limiting device with the attitude and heading indicators covered
Arrive within 5 minutes of the planned time
Hold the en route altitude within 200 feet
Name the attitude before any control input

activities.why: The point A to B pieces are the AIH's own example [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Conditions are the rules for the demonstration: equipment, references and limits; criteria measure whether the objective was met [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. The instrument pieces come from this lesson's sample [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

activities.title: True or false: instructional aids
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Instructional aids are self-supporting and can carry a lesson without the instructor.
cards.why: False. Aids are not self-supporting; they support, supplement or reinforce what is taught [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

cards.s: If a two-dimensional picture does the job, it should be used instead of a model.
Because aids go with a spoken presentation, the words on them should be kept to a minimum.
An ATD may be used for parts of the CFII practical test.
cards.why: False. ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

cards.s: The FAA recommends training in the simulator until the tasks are done successfully, before trying them in the aircraft.
Aids should be checked before use for completeness and technical accuracy.
cards.why: True. It is one of the AIH guidelines for effective aids (Figure 5-17) [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].

activities.title: Read the nose-high panel
activities.intro: Drag each teaching point to the instrument it belongs to on IFH Figure 7-39.

pins.label: Decreasing here picks the nose-high recovery
Quick level reference, unless past its limits or failed
Needle reverses and stops: level pitch
Level its miniature aircraft and center the ball
Covered with the attitude indicator for partial panel
Shows a climb; reads the opposite way when nose-low

activities.why: Airspeed decreasing calls for the nose-high recovery, and the reversal and stabilization of the airspeed and altimeter needles show level pitch [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The attitude indicator helps in moderate attitudes but may have exceeded its limits or failed [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The turn coordinator's level miniature aircraft and centered ball show straight, coordinated flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Partial panel covers the attitude gyro and heading indicator [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. Nose-low attitudes show on the same instruments in the opposite direction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

activities.title: The nose-low recovery, by the numbers
activities.intro: Put the IFH steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Airspeed increasing: recognize a nose-low attitude
Reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and altitude loss
Level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, by the turn coordinator
Raise the nose to level flight with smooth back elevator pressure
Keep a fast cross-check for overcontrol as the needles slow and reverse
Add the attitude indicator to the cross-check, if available, as the others stabilize
Return to the assigned altitude once stabilized
activities.why: Sequence from [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]: power, bank, pitch, then a fast cross-check for overcontrol, then the attitude indicator and the return to the assigned altitude. In initial training the recovery is made by the numbers in that order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

activities.title: The evaluator picks steep turns
activities.intro: On the CFII practical test the evaluator says: "Teach me steep turns as your instrument student." Make each call.

steps.s: You have a library plan for steep turns. What do you do first?
options: Ask who the student is: hours, last lesson, airplane
Read the plan aloud word for word from the top
Recite the PTS tolerances for steep turns
Put the plan away and talk from memory
steps.why: The explanation is based on the learner's known experience and knowledge [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], and a flight lesson plan should fit the particular learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

steps.s: How do you open the lesson?
options: A joke about checkrides to break the ice
The full list of common errors, before anything else
A question about the maneuver, why it matters, then the objective
The history of the attitude indicator
steps.why: The introduction is attention (related to the subject; unrelated jokes distract), motivation and an overview with the objective [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

steps.s: In what order do you describe the elements?
options: Common errors first, then the steps in any order
Partial panel first, then the full panel
Roll-out first, since that is where errors show
Entry, the turn, recovery: the order flown, each with its error
steps.why: Explain a skill in the same step-by-step order used to perform it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Going from the full panel the learner knows to partial panel follows known to unknown [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

steps.s: The student asks: "What if the vacuum pump quits during the turn?"
options: Say it is not part of today's lesson
Answer, and include the partial panel steep turn in the brief
Tell the student to look outside instead
Promise to cover it after the checkride
steps.why: The PTS steep turn Task asks for entry and recovery using full panel and partial panel, and the IFH flies every analog maneuver except the takeoff with the gyros covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. Practicing without the attitude and heading indicators prepares for a vacuum failure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

steps.s: You want to show the bank and the cross-check. Which aids?
options: Eight slides with every IFH paragraph
No aids, since words are always clearer
A panel figure and the model, on the key points only
The whole POH, page by page
steps.why: Aids go on the key points, stay simple and use few words [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]; a model is easy to handle and invites questions [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

steps.s: Time to wrap up the brief.
options: Retrace the elements against the objective and take questions
Introduce the steep spiral as a bonus maneuver
Skip the summary to save time for flying
Read out the PTS errors list one more time
steps.why: The conclusion retraces the important elements and relates them to the objective, with no new ideas [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]; invite questions before leaving the explanation phase [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

activities.title: Numbers you will put in your plans
activities.intro: Work it out with the IFH method, then type your answer.

items.q: Using the IFH rule of 15 percent of true airspeed, about what bank angle gives a standard rate turn at 110 knots?
items.why: Divide the airspeed by 10 and add half the result: 11 + 5.5 = 16.5 degrees [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The IFH example is 100 knots, about 15 degrees [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

items.q: A standard rate turn is 3 degrees per second. How many seconds does a timed standard rate turn from 090 to 210 take?
At half standard rate, how many seconds does a 90 degree timed turn take?
items.why: Half standard rate is 1.5 degrees per second, the IFH example being 45 degrees in 30 seconds: 90 / 1.5 = 60 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

items.q: After a partial panel recovery on a PFD, your learner is 250 feet below the assigned altitude. Using the IFH rule of thumb, what vertical speed should she use to climb back?
items.why: Use a vertical speed about double the altitude deviation: 2 x 250 = 500 fpm, but never more than the airplane's optimum rate of climb or descent [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
